paragraphs.text: A loose [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition) from the 1990s, kept in Guangzhou and stored the old way. It was not pressed into cakes. The leaf was [packed into bamboo baskets](liu-bao:making-traditional) lined with bamboo leaves, and the basket lets the tea breathe, so it goes on changing through the decades it rests.

Liu Bao is the [dark tea](dark:definition) of [Guangxi](guangxi:where-it-is), named for Liubao town in Cangwu County, near Wuzhou. Its leaf is piled after it is made, so warmth, moisture and microbes can slowly change it. The region's [warm, wet climate](guangxi:land-and-climate) is part of the reason it is made here: the trade links that steady damp to the slow ageing the style is kept for.

At over thirty years, this lot is well past the ten the trade needs before it counts a Liu Bao as [aged](liu-bao:age-aged), and how a tea was stored matters as much as how long. Guangzhou has long been part of the style's story. The tea went by boat down the river to Wuzhou, on to Guangzhou, and out by sea to the Chinese workers of the [Southeast Asian tin mines](liu-bao:nanyang-trade).

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
